title: Guardrails for Agent Output: Lint and Sandboxes
description: Nine tools that constrain what an agent can produce and reach: slop-detecting lint rules, declared sandbox tiers, cheaper crawling and signed messaging.

tldr: Agent guardrails work best when the boundary is explicit. ai-deslop rejects slop patterns in CI, plimsoll declares the isolation tier each run executed behind, Jevcrawl filters pages before the LLM reads them, Aweb signs agent-to-agent messages, and Skills Hub keeps agent skills identical across every tool you run.
content:
# Guardrails for Agent Output: Lint, Sandboxes, Crawling and Memory

The most useful guardrails are not the ones that try to understand what an agent meant. They are the ones that state a boundary in a form a machine can check. A lint rule either fires or it does not. A sandbox tier is either strong enough or it is not. A message is either signed by the agent you expected or it is not. The nine tools below all take that approach, and together they cover the four places agent output tends to go wrong: the code it writes, the environment it runs in, the web it reads, and what it remembers afterwards.

## Lint the slop out of generated TypeScript

Most teams reviewing AI-generated code are looking for the same handful of patterns: chained type assertions that fabricate evidence, conditional empty object spreads to quietly omit fields, known values widened to unknown, runtime typeof checks standing in for real parsing. [[link:/tools/1649|ai-deslop]] turns that list into Oxlint rules under a single namespace.

It installs as an oxlint JavaScript plugin and works on Bun, Deno and Node runtimes. The value over a style guide is that it fails in CI, which means the pattern never reaches review. The cost is that the vendored rules expect your oxlint version to stay in sync, and the defaults are opinionated enough that most repositories will want to tune them.

## Declare the wall the code ran behind

Running code an agent wrote is a different risk from reading it. [[link:/tools/1617|Plimsoll]] runs untrusted code inside a sandbox and, crucially, reports the isolation boundary each run executed behind. Isolation is expressed as one of four tiers, weakest first, and a request can demand a minimum tier: if the sandbox is weaker than requested, nothing runs at all.

That last detail is what separates it from a sandbox that merely exists. A guarantee you cannot check is a preference. A guarantee a request can demand is a control.

## Crawl for the answer, not for the pages

Giving an agent web access usually means feeding it pages and hoping. [[link:/tools/1621|Jevcrawl]] is an MCP server and CLI that inverts the order: a small decision model picks every link and every passage, so the agent's LLM reads only what answers its question. The authors report finding the answer page about twice as often as Crawl4AI and roughly $0.025 per task, measured against WebWalkerQA.

Filtering before the frontier model sees anything is the same economic argument as caching, applied to crawling. The claims are the project's own, so reproduce them on your own documentation before relying on the numbers.

## Memory that survives the session

An agent that forgets everything between runs needs its context rebuilt every time. [[link:/tools/1620|MemorySync]] is infrastructure for that: it ingests from multiple sources, builds a memory graph with tiering, and handles retrieval, context assembly and adaptive orchestration, with connectors for [[link:/tools/93|LangChain]], LangGraph, LlamaIndex, [[link:/tools/56|CrewAI]], Pydantic AI and the Vercel AI SDK.

It is aimed at production systems rather than single-agent projects, and the governance layer is the part most teams will care about once memory stops being per-user.

## Agents that can message each other

Once you run more than one agent, they need to coordinate. [[link:/tools/1661|Aweb]] gives each agent a name and an inbox, holds messages until the agent reads them, and signs every message so the receiver can check who sent an instruction before acting on it. Agents wake where they already run, including [[link:/tools/1487|Claude Code]], Codex, Pi, ChatGPT and Claude, so nothing polls and no turn is wasted checking an empty inbox. It is MIT licensed and self-hostable, with paid plans alongside the free tier.

## Install a skill once

Agent skills are only useful if every tool agrees on them. [[link:/tools/1657|Skills Hub]] is a cross-platform desktop app that installs a skill once and syncs it to the global skills directories of the coding tools and projects you use, on macOS, Windows and Linux. You can browse task-focused collections in the app or import from Git and local folders.

## Documentation that answers for itself

A large share of agent questions are answered by documentation that already exists. [[link:/tools/1658|DocFlare AI]] adds a streaming retrieval-augmented answer box to a docs site with a single script tag, citing the sources it used. It runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers AI, Vectorize and D1, so there is no OpenAI key, no external vector database and no server to operate. The trade-off is that it is tied to the Cloudflare stack and answer quality follows Workers AI models.

## A task list the agent can actually read

[[link:/tools/1660|GSD Task Manager]] is an offline-first Eisenhower matrix with a drag-and-drop four-quadrant board, quick capture, search and keyboard navigation, optional PocketBase sync, and an MCP server. The MCP server is the interesting part: your agent reads and updates the same list you do, instead of maintaining a parallel notion of what matters today.

## An agent that asks first

[[link:/tools/1626|NanoMuse]] is an open-source personal agent for every device you own, with a name and appearance of its own. It keeps working while the application is closed, remembers you over time, and asks before doing anything you would care about. That last property is a guardrail of a different kind: instead of constraining the environment, it constrains the agent's own initiative.

## Where to start

If you run agents that write code, start with ai-deslop and plimsoll, because together they cover the two failure modes that actually cost money: bad code merged, and untrusted code executed. Add Jevcrawl if your agents read the web. Add Aweb and MemorySync once you have more than one agent working on the same problem, and add GSD Task Manager or NanoMuse when the agent needs a shared notion of what to do next.
